title: One optimisation step
prompt: Put the steps of **one** mini-batch update in the order PyTorch needs them.
items: Run the forward pass to get predictions
Update the parameters with the optimizer
hints: Gradients accumulate by default, so something has to reset them before they are filled again.
explanation: `zero_grad()` first so `backward()` does not add to stale gradients; forward → loss → `backward()` fills `.grad`; `step()` finally consumes it.

title: Match the activation to its property
prompt: Pick the property that fits each activation function. A property can be used more than once.
explanation: Sigmoid and hard sigmoid both squash to $(0, 1)$, so that property is the right answer for two rows.

title: Does the layer have trainable parameters?
prompt: Drag each layer into the right bucket. One chip does not belong in either.
explanation: Pooling, activations, flatten and dropout are fixed functions. `BatchNorm2d` has a learnable scale and shift, and `Embedding` is a learnable lookup table. `SGD` is not a layer at all.

title: Back-of-the-envelope speed-up (±2% accepted)
prompt: An epoch takes 125 s on one GPU and 34 s on four. What is the speed-up (old time / new time)? Answers within **2 %** are accepted.
explanation: $125 / 34 \approx 3.68$. Perfect linear scaling would give 4, so there is some overhead.

correct = 0

title: Why shuffle the training data?
prompt: In two or three sentences: why do we usually **shuffle** the training set every epoch?
modelAnswer: If the data arrive in a fixed order (for example sorted by class), every mini-batch is biased and consecutive gradient steps pull in the same direction. Shuffling makes each mini-batch a better estimate of the full gradient and stops the network from learning the order.

rubric.text: Mini-batches become representative samples of the whole data set
Avoids correlated / biased consecutive gradient steps (e.g. data sorted by class)
Mentions that the model should not exploit the order of the examples
